title: Causal explanation of gate failure stated as fact in abstract
quote:
so the model imitates
terse references and loses reasoning, which makes the gate a weak control
explanation: The abstract states as a conclusion that the model 'imitates terse references and loses reasoning'. The evidence is three correlates (unchanged boxed share, lower accuracy among boxed answers, 3.2x shorter outputs). Section 2 admits for the closely related Kim et al. result that 'we did not test its cause'. Other implementation-level explanations are left open: the 512-token training limit that includes the prompt cuts 24-26% of kept solutions and removes their final answer and end token, the loss covers the prompt, and the gold is stored without a delimiter. None of these is separated from imitation of terse references, so this mechanism is a hypothesis presented as a finding.

title: Failed positive gate means the null is uninterpretable, not 'a null for the recipe'
quote:
No arm improves, not even training on reference
solutions, so this is a null for the recipe, not a statement about self-training.
explanation: The sentence uses the gold arm's failure (-32.2) as if it strengthened the null ('not even'). A positive control that fails shows the pipeline cannot register improvement even when the training signal is as good as it gets. It is therefore evidence of a pipeline defect (truncation, prompt-in-loss, token cap, storage defect) and not just of a weak control. The abstract concedes the gate is weak, but the contribution list still presents a clean null for 'the recipe'. The recipe as run has several choices that are probably unrepresentative (lr 1e-5 'our code's default and not tuned', 512 cap equal to the training limit, prompt loss), so the null may reflect this implementation and not the generate-verify-train recipe the title names.

title: Final-round declines are asserted as real while below the stated detectable effect
quote:
pass@1 falls 3.2–4.8
points in each of three seeds (mean −4.1). The design detects only gains
of about 10 points of pass@1 (6 in the ﬁnal round).
explanation: Nulls on gains are justified by intervals and power, but the abstract treats a -4.1 mean drop as a finding although the stated minimum detectable effect in that round is about 6 points. No interval for the drop is given in the abstract, so a reader cannot tell whether it excludes zero. The paper also notes that intervals omit training-seed variance and that a replicate pair differs by 3.8 points. A drop of 3-5 points is of the size of that unmodelled variance. The paper applies a stricter standard to gains than to losses. The final round also uses a 'revised recipe' added after seeing the earlier nulls, so the decline is post hoc and not comparable to the 'any of four learning rates' null in the preceding sentence.

title: Learning-rate null overstated: sweep is confounded with k and rounds
quote:
no gain is detectable on a held-out exam at any learning rate we tried (a coarse grid that
also changes k and rounds)
explanation: The abstract speaks of 'four learning rates' as if it were a clean learning-rate sweep. The contribution list admits the grid also changes k and rounds, and Section 3.3 says most evidence comes from higher-rate runs listed only in a supplementary table. Learning rate is therefore not isolated, and 'no gain at any learning rate' cannot be read as covering the learning-rate dimension. With the same weak power (10 points), this supports 'we saw no large gain in the configurations tried' and not a null over learning rate. The abstract does not give this caveat.

title: Claim that SFT loop 'does not' improve accuracy contradicts the power caveat
quote: These studies improve accuracy, which our SFT loop does not
explanation: Related Work contrasts RLVR studies that improve accuracy with an SFT loop that 'does not'. Elsewhere the paper says its design detects only gains of about 10 pass@1 points (6 in the final round), with optimistic thresholds, and that gains below this 'could have been missed'. The data show only that no gain was detected, not that none exists. The comparison with RLVR is also not matched: one adapter per round from the base model, 1 epoch, lr 1e-5 and a 512-token cap versus GRPO with online rollouts. The sentence suggests an SFT-versus-RL difference that the experiments cannot establish.

title: Self-inflicted storage bug framed as verifier bias; scope of 'the verifier' question
quote:
A format probe that re-renders gold answers in valid forms shows that \dfrac
and \tfrac are always rejected
explanation: The title, abstract and Section 3.2 heading ('the Verifier and Its Directional Bias') frame the study around what 'the verifier accepts'. The dominant defect (rejecting 15.5-18.3% of accepted generations, 94-98% of correct answers on affected problems, with 29-34 of those problems having unparseable golds) comes from the authors' own storage of gold answers without a delimiter, not from math-verify's judgement. Independent measurement on real solutions gives a 7.8% false-negative rate, and the cited work reports 0.95 recall for math-verify on MATH. The introduction's 'frequent verifier defect' and the abstract's one-in-six figure present a pipeline bug as evidence about verifier-filtered training. The abstract partly admits the audit is uninformative, but the framing still raises the expectation that the verifier question is being tested. Also, the 8-of-10 'probably the gold-storage defect' is an untested attribution.

title: Decomposition listed as a contribution though it follows Xu et al. and is hedged elsewhere
quote:
A decomposition of an accuracy decline under a ﬁxed token cap into a
ﬁnished-accuracy part and a cap-share part
explanation: Related Work says the separation of finished accuracy from termination is motivated by Xu et al. [15], who identify 'a ﬁxed token cap under style drift' as a measurement failure, and states that the per-round false-reject measurement and the patch are not claimed as contributions. The decomposition is presented as a contribution without the same disclaimer. Also, the contribution states that finished generations lose 5.5-10.6 points at the highest rate, but the introduction says 'on one seed the cap share carries more of it', and conditioning on finished generations is a selected subset whose composition differs between the trained and untrained model. 'The same problem mix' only partly addresses this. The bullet is more confident than the text supports.

title: Pre-registration framing overstates what was fixed in advance
quote: We ﬁxed four measures in advance
explanation: The paper then says the reading rule can only fire if accuracy rises, and that the higher learning rates, the controls, the primary accuracy measure, the termination measures, re-scoring and the final round were all added after seeing earlier runs. Of the headline results (abstract), the final-round decline, the gate, the boxed/accuracy decomposition and the audit are all post hoc. The sentence about prespecified measures suggests more confirmatory structure than exists; further, the pre-set rule could not detect the observed outcome (declines), so no prespecified test bears on the main findings. The abstract does not mark which results are post hoc.

title: Unclear relation between 'patched verifier', V and V′; Run B definition
quote:
Every table grades all runs with V ′ , which the loop used
only in the ﬁnal round
explanation: The patch is defined as rewriting \dfrac and \tfrac to \frac 'and nothing else'. V′ is defined separately as wrapping the gold in \boxed{} when the prediction contains one. The abstract says 'one patched veriﬁer' and Run B is 'patched veriﬁer', so it is unclear whether V′ includes the dfrac patch, whether Run B's selection used the dfrac patch or V′, and which is applied in the regrade of Run A versus B. The A-versus-B contrast is described as the central control, and the reader cannot tell if the two arms differ in the dfrac rewrite (0-4 examples) or in V′ (+23% pool). The A-B difference of the selection verifier is the central comparison, so this must be explicit.

title: 'Held-out' exams and 'common form of the loop' overgeneralise
quote:
We study the question
in a cheap and common form of the loop, oﬄine rejection-sampling SFT
explanation: The abstract describes 'held-out MATH-500 and GSM8K exams'. Design P selects and evaluates on the same 1,000 problems, so those results are not held-out, and in Design I the 150-problem exam is a 30% partition of a single 500-problem set while generation runs on all 500. The final 500-problem round's held-out status is not described in this part. In addition, 'common' is asserted for a recipe with unusual settings: restart-from-base fresh adapters each round, one epoch, lr 1e-5, loss on the prompt, 512-token sequence limit including prompt, LoRA on q and v only. The cited loops (STaR, ReST-EM, RFT) differ in these. The scope of the title, 'One Verifier-Filtered Self-Training Recipe', is more cautious than 'common', so the introduction contradicts it.

title: Claim that pass@8 stays within 4 points contradicted by Table 2
quote: pass@8 ends within 4 points of round 0 in every run
explanation: Section 4.2 says pass@8 ends within 4 points of round 0 in every Design I run at 10^-5. In Table 2 (last round R4, k = 8), the pass@k column for run B at seed 0 is -5.3 [-12.0, +2.0], which is outside the 4-point band. Run B at seed 0 is a 10^-5 run, so the statement is false for at least one run. The error understates the largest coverage loss in the headline 'small declines' summary, and the sentence is then used to support 'we read this as a possible small decline'.

title: 'Correct' is said to be judged by the selecting verifier, but all evaluation uses a different verifier V'
quote: means accepted by the veriﬁer (preset reward), the same veriﬁer that selects the
explanation: Section 3.4 defines correctness as acceptance by 'the same verifier that selects the training data'. Section 3.2 says that every table regrades all runs with V', which the loop itself used only in the final round. Run A, Run C and Design P selected training data with the original verifier, so for them evaluation and selection verifiers differ. Only Run B (and the final round) satisfy the stated definition. This matters for the paper's central question ('better at mathematics or only at what the verifier accepts'): the measured quantity is acceptance by V', not by the training-time reward. Under V' the A-versus-B comparison also has the original-verifier arm graded by a verifier it never saw, which the text never discusses as a mismatch. The definition should be made per run or the sentence corrected.

title: Round-0 regrade jump (33.3 to 40.0) is not reconcilable with the claimed negligible patch effect
quote: pass@1 40.0 against 33.3 for Run A at seed 1
explanation: Regrading the untrained model with V' raises round-0 pass@1 by 6.7 points, about 10 of 150 exam problems. Section 4.3 argues the patch is nearly inert: \dfrac appears in 0.50-0.73% of generations (roughly one exam problem for a single draw), and kept pools differ by at most 4 of 872 examples. These two facts cannot both come from the same patch unless V' contains other changes (timeout retries, other normalisations) that are never decomposed. A reader cannot tell which verifier component moves accuracy by 6.7 points, nor whether those components also change pool composition between arms A and B. If the other changes are as large as the round-0 shift suggests, the 'patch control could not detect an effect' conclusion and the 'pools differ by at most 4' statement need re-derivation. A per-component attribution of the original-to-V' shift is missing.
related_sections: 4.3 The Patch Control Could Not Detect an Effect

title: Training truncation removes the verified answer from 24-26% of pool examples, so training data are no longer verifier-accepted
quote: any kept solution longer than about 512 tokens minus the prompt length is cut
explanation: Pool membership is decided by the verifier on the full generation (up to 512 new tokens). The training limit of 512 tokens includes the prompt, so the paper itself reports that 24-26% of the round-0 pool is cut in training and loses its final answer and end-of-sequence token. For those examples the object trained on is a truncated, unfinished solution that the verifier never accepted; the filter no longer certifies what the model learns. The model is also taught that long solutions end without an answer or EOS, which can raise the cap-hit share and lower accuracy, an effect indistinguishable from 'drift toward the verifier'. This is an implementation defect in the recipe rather than a property of verifier-filtered self-training, yet the paper frames its conclusion as a null for the recipe. The additional choice of computing loss over the prompt too (and no per-problem cap, so easy problems contribute up to k examples each) further departs from the standard rejection-sampling fine-tuning recipe. There is no ablation that drops or re-packs over-length examples to show the declines survive.

title: A 'seed' is said to set training randomness, but the trainer seed is fixed at 42
quote: A “seed” sets the exam partition, the selection set and
explanation: Section 3.3 states that a seed sets the exam partition, the selection set and the training randomness together. Section 3.4 lists 'trainer seed 42' among the library defaults used for every run. If the trainer seed is constant, training randomness (LoRA init, data order) is not varied by the experiment seed, or at least the paper does not say how the two interact. This affects interpretation of every pair the paper uses as a 'replicate' to gauge training-seed variance, because partition variance and training variance are then confounded differently from what is stated. Reproducibility also suffers: it is unclear which random sources a reader must set to reproduce a run.

title: The 3.8-point replicate gap used to calibrate training-seed variance cannot be traced to the reported tables
quote: as a gauge ends 3.8 points of sample accuracy apart
explanation: The paper uses a 'replicate pair' that ends 3.8 points of sample accuracy apart as its only gauge for variance missing from the bootstrap intervals, and it also argues the detectable-effect thresholds are optimistic because of it. The pair is not identified. In the main text, same-configuration changes in sample accuracy at 10^-5 differ by at most 1.6 points (A: -3.3 vs -3.1; B: -4.2 vs -2.6), at 2x10^-4 by 0.0, and at 10^-4 by at most 2.4; the only larger gap is at 5x10^-4 (-10.8 vs -6.0, 4.8) and in round-0 levels (41.0 vs 37.7, 3.3). None gives 3.8, so the reader cannot check which two runs it refers to or whether it is a change or a level. With a gauge based on one pair, and one that mixes partition and training variance, the size of the missing variance term is essentially unquantified, which weakens the 'optimistic threshold' argument in both directions.

title: Counting A and B runs as independent evidence overstates the support for a decline in sample accuracy
quote: pass@1 is 3.3–4.7 points lower at round 4, with every interval including zero (Table 2); sample accuracy falls 2.6–4.2 points, with an interval excluding zero for three of the
explanation: Section 4.2 reports that the sample-accuracy interval excludes zero for three of four runs and treats this as the basis for a possible decline. The four runs are not four independent observations. A and B at the same seed share the exam partition, the round-0 draws and (per Section 4.3) nearly identical pools, so they are close to replicates of two experiments; the paper says as much about the patch control and in Section 3.4 ('the runs are not independent'). The bootstrap intervals also exclude training-seed variance, which the paper itself measures as comparable to the effect (B minus A flips from +5.3 to -5.3 in pass@1 for near-identical pools). No multiplicity correction is applied across the many metrics, rates and runs. In this setting 'three of four intervals exclude zero' is roughly 'one or two experiments with narrow, optimistic intervals', and the pass@1 and pass@k intervals for the same runs all include zero. The text hedges ('possible small decline'), but the stated count still lends more weight than the design supports.

title: Evidence for 'several rounds' and for an effective learning rate never overlap
quote: default and was not tuned
explanation: The five-round (four adapters) runs use 10^-5, a learning rate for LoRA that is one to two orders below typical values; the paper itself says the adapter changed the MATH-500 outputs little and that unchanged length and cap-hit share are weak evidence the adapter did little. The runs at rates that clearly change behaviour (10^-4 to 5x10^-4) have only three rounds (two adapters) and k = 4. So the study never tests many rounds at a rate where each round has an effect, which is what the framing 'after several generate-verify-train rounds' and the 'null result for one recipe' suggest. The 10^-5 declines also come from runs where the adapter hardly moved the model, so they say little about self-training either way, and the paper concedes the runs differ in k, rounds, pool size and metric so that only 10^-4 to 5x10^-4 isolates the rate. A null at insufficient exposure is weaker than the title implies; the limits of this coverage should be stated next to the headline claim.

title: pass@1 and pass@k changes for run A, seed 0 have identical point estimates and intervals
explanation: In Table 2 the first row (A, seed 0, 10^-5) gives exactly the same value and interval, -3.3 [-10.7, +4.0], for both Delta pass@1 and Delta pass@k. pass@1 is a single draw per problem while pass@8 is the best of eight, so problem-level paired differences should differ; identical bootstrap intervals to the first decimal require identical paired data. This could be a coincidence (both could reflect the same 5 problems changing), but pass@k then would equal pass@1 under the added/lost definition only by chance, and the column could also be a copy-paste error. Please verify against bootstrap_ci.py output, since the table is the basis for the 'every interval includes zero' conclusions.

title: Primary outcome is capped by a verifier defect that rejects nearly all correct answers on roughly 11-12% of problems
quote: it rejects 94–98% of correct answers in every round
explanation: The verifier treatment states that on the 54-62 problems (of 500) where the gold-storage defect fires, 94-98% of correct answers are rejected, and for 29-34 of them the gold cannot be parsed by the original verifier at all. V' repairs the dfrac issue but, per the paper's own account, not this defect, so about 11-12% of problems (about 16-19 of 150 exam problems) cannot be scored correct whatever the model does. Every accuracy, pass@k and interval in Tables 1-2 is therefore bounded and noisier than reported, the effective exam is closer to 130 problems, and the detectable-effect formula (based on half-widths over 150 problems) mixes in problems that cannot contribute signal. The defect is also a verifier failure of exactly the type the paper's title question is about, yet the main analysis neither excludes these problems nor reports results restricted to problems with a usable gold and working acceptance. The paper notes the defect and defers to an appendix, but the absence of a clean-subset analysis in the primary comparison leaves the 'mathematics versus verifier' question confounded with the verifier's own defect.

title: pass@8 claim contradicted by Table 2
quote: pass@8 ends within 4 points of round 0 in every run
explanation: Table 2 (10^-5 rows) gives pass@k changes of -3.3, -1.3, -5.3 (B, seed 0), -2.0 and -2.7. The B seed-0 run falls 5.3 points, outside the stated 4-point band. The sentence is used to support the 'small declines' reading of Design I, so the stated range is wrong as written (the maximum drop is 5.3).

title: 'Finished accuracy carries the whole change' not supported by Table 2
quote: does not rise and ﬁnished accuracy carries the whole change
explanation: At 1e-4 the matched finished-accuracy changes in Table 2 are -1.3, -0.6, -1.0 (all intervals include zero), while sample accuracy falls 3.7, 4.7, 2.3. At 2e-4 they are -2.6 and -3.2 (intervals include zero) against sample-accuracy falls of 6.0 and 6.0. The matched finished measure therefore explains well under half of the fall and is not distinguishable from zero. Claiming that it carries 'the whole change' overstates; the remainder (problem-mix, other shifts) is unexplained. This also bears on the cap-share decomposition, whose fractions cannot be reconciled with the matched measure from the tables shown.

title: Cap-share decomposition fractions reported inconsistently and not reconcilable
quote: attributes 12–30% of the decline to the cap share in the three
explanation: Section 4.5 gives 12-30% for the three seed-1 runs plus '-2 and 5%' for two further runs, and 52-72% at seed 2. Section 5.3 restates only '12-30% in the three seed-1 runs and 52-72% at seed 2' and drops the two further runs (one with a negative share, i.e. the cap share offsetting the decline). Which runs are 'original seed-1' is not stated in the main text. Using Table 2 directly (finished matched vs sample accuracy, e.g. A seed 2: -1.5 of -6.0, implying ~75% from cap/other) the seed-2 range 52-72% is not reproduced, and the seed-1 split also cannot be derived. A 20-point difference in cap share between seeds that share a recipe is itself evidence of seed-level noise, undercutting the interpretive weight placed on the split.

title: Gate is not a valid positive control for self-training; failure attributed causally without test
quote: must raise accuracy for the recipe to count as able to help
explanation: Training an instruction-tuned model on 300 terse human reference solutions is an off-policy, different-distribution task from training on the model's own filtered samples. A drop of 32 points with massive style shift ($-spans 4% to 98%, 3.2x shorter) shows that imitating those solutions hurts, not that the recipe cannot improve accuracy when given correct on-policy data. The paper later states 'The model imitates terse reference solutions and loses reasoning steps' as a mechanism, but this is inferred from correlated length/style changes only; no ablation (e.g. reference solutions rewritten in the model's style, or gold final answers only) separates style imitation from damage by the recipe. The inference 'the loop's decline cannot be attributed to self-training or to the verifier' relies on a gate whose validity as a positive control is assumed rather than established.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: Unsupported mechanism for gold failure (imitation of terse solutions)
quote: imitates terse reference solutions and loses reasoning steps
explanation: The evidence is a drop in median length (1,332 to 414 characters) and unchanged boxed share, with accuracy among boxed answers falling from 48.5 to 17.1%. Shorter output and lower accuracy co-occur, but 'loses reasoning steps' is not measured (no step counts or error analysis), and conditioning on boxed answers is itself post-treatment selection. The statement should be hedged as a hypothesis.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: Mixed metrics in the gate paragraph do not reconcile
quote: accuracy among them falls from 48.5 to 17.1%
explanation: The same paragraph quotes pass@1 49.2% to 17.0% (V') and, for the string-match grader, boxed share 90.6 to 90.3% and accuracy among boxed 48.5 to 17.1%. Multiplying gives about 43.9% and 15.4% sample accuracy, i.e. a 5-point gap to the quoted pass@1 at round 0 and a 1.6-point gap after training, and a decline of about -28.5 rather than -32.2. Different graders and different statistics (pass@1 vs mean sample accuracy) are mixed without saying so, so a reader cannot check that 'not a format defect' follows from the numbers. The paper should state which grader/metric each figure uses and give the like-for-like decline.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: Cross-seed t interval excludes zero but paper declines to claim a cost; inconsistent standard
quote: we do not claim that it costs accuracy or isolate the cause
explanation: The three-seed mean change is -4.1 pass@1 with t interval [-6.1, -2.1] and -4.5 sample accuracy [-8.0, -1.0]; every seed is negative and all three sample-accuracy intervals exclude zero. These are the only intervals that include training-seed variance and they exclude zero. Elsewhere the paper writes that 'every A/B run declines' on the basis of single-seed bootstrap intervals. The hedge is defensible (shared exam draw, n=3, single rate) but the standard is applied unevenly, and the 'null result' title/abstract framing sits uneasily with a consistent, interval-excluding-zero decline. The text should say plainly whether the evidence is for harm, and why the same hedge is not applied at 5e-4.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Revised Recipe

title: Undefined comparison figures in the injected-bias control
quote: against −3.7, −2.7 and −5.5 in the three unbiased seeds
explanation: The reference numbers are not defined. Earlier in the section the boxed-share changes in the three unbiased seeds are given as -0.6, -0.6 and -5.1 points; here -3.7, -2.7 and -5.5 are offered as the comparable quantity to a 'difference' of +2.8 (affected-minus-other change). The reader must infer these are the corresponding between-group differences in the unbiased runs, defined by the same \frac split, and that they differ from the overall shares. Without this stated, the claim that the biased run shows no selective avoidance cannot be checked. In addition, the biased run's difference (+2.8, interval [-2.8, +8.3]) is only compared to point estimates of single seeds with no intervals.

title: Gold arm used as a null-drift reference for r_t despite large distribution shift
quote: so rt drifts as much as the falls we observe
explanation: The argument is that train-on-gold, with no verifier in the loop, raises r_t by 2.1-3.3 points, hence r_t changes of 1.5-2.6 in self-training runs are unrelated to the verifier. But the gold arm changes the model drastically (style adoption, 3.2x shorter outputs, pass@1 -32), so its r_t movement mainly reflects boxed-share and answer-form shifts, not baseline drift. The gold intervals ([-1.2, 8.1], [-2.2, 6.7]) also include zero, so 'rises' is an estimate with no support. The comparison cannot establish that the observed falls are noise; it merely shows r_t is unstable under large behavioural change. The paper itself notes elsewhere that the audit has no valid positive control.

title: A failed positive gate makes the null uninformative, not 'scoped to this recipe'
quote: Because no arm improves and the positive
explanation: The paper infers that because no arm improves and the gate failed, 'the null belongs to this recipe'. That inference runs the wrong way. A positive control that fails shows the pipeline (LoRA SFT, 512-token cap, fresh adapter per round, this exam) could not be shown to produce a gain even when given a supervision source that is supposed to help. That makes the null uninformative about whether the recipe works. It does not confine the null to the recipe. A failed control is also not evidence about the recipe itself. The gate is run only under the revised recipe and the 500-problem exam, while the four-learning-rate null comes from earlier runs under a different recipe and 150 problems. The paper's own conclusion calls it an 'inconclusive null', which fits the logic better than the abstract and contributions do. Credit is due for stating that the gate is a weak control. The scoping claim still outruns what the gate supports.

title: Abstract and title frame a recipe-level null; conclusion calls it inconclusive and the data show a decline
quote: The null therefore concerns this recipe only.
explanation: The abstract and title present a 'null result' that 'concerns this recipe'. The conclusion says that, because the gate failed, 'this is an inconclusive null for the recipe and says little about self-training'. The abstract also reports that the final-round loop lowers pass@1 in all three seeds (mean -4.1, t interval [-6.1, -2.1] excluding zero). A decline whose interval excludes zero is not a null. The text sits between 'null for the recipe' (abstract, contributions), 'inconclusive' (conclusion) and a measured negative effect (Section 4.6). A reader cannot tell which claim the paper stands behind. The framing should be reconciled. Either call it an inconclusive/negative result, or state what the gate failure does and does not license.

title: Standard applied asymmetrically: 'no gain' is a finding but 'consistent decline' is not claimed
quote: we do not claim that it costs accuracy or isolate the cause.
explanation: Three seeds all decline in pass@1 and in sample accuracy. The three sample-accuracy intervals all exclude zero, and the mean pass@1 t interval [-6.1, -2.1] excludes zero. The second grader reproduces the sign and size. Yet the paper declines to say the loop costs accuracy, while the abstract states the 'no gain' null from intervals that include zero. The caveats given are legitimate: three seeds, one exam draw, one rate, and no seed variance in the intervals. The same caveats apply to the null side, whose power is also computed without seed variance. The abstract therefore leaves the impression of a flat null and plays down the only statistically supported effect in the paper, which is negative. The paper should state the same evidentiary standard for both directions.

title: 'Not a format defect' contradicts the later concession that a format artefact is not ruled out
quote: It is not a format defect: on the 500 exam problems
explanation: The gate failure is declared 'not a format defect' because the share of generations with a \boxed answer is unchanged. Section 5.1 then concedes that the string-match grader 'does not rule out a format artefact in the gate'. The model also adopts the reference style almost completely ($-delimited spans in 1,577 of 1,600 generations), and there are many ways a boxed answer can still be graded wrong. These include a different answer form inside \boxed (units, \text{}, $ signs, \dfrac, ordering), and failure of both math-verify and string match on the new form. An unchanged boxed share excludes only one format failure (missing \boxed). The 32-point collapse, at a low learning rate such as 2e-5 and with a 1.5B instruct model, also looks large enough to leave a training-pipeline problem possible. The categorical statement in 4.6 and the abstract should be weakened to match the concession.

title: Causal explanation of the gate failure ('loses reasoning steps') is asserted, not tested
quote: model imitates terse reference solutions and loses reasoning steps; the three
explanation: The evidence is a drop in median character length (3.2x) and in accuracy among boxed answers. The abstract states the mechanism as fact: 'the model imitates terse references and loses reasoning'. No analysis ties the accuracy loss to lost reasoning steps. For example, there is no control on solution length, no per-problem comparison of reasoning content, and no check of whether the shorter outputs are wrong because of omitted steps or because of answer-form mismatch. The paper uses the claimed mechanism to separate the gate's decline from the loop's decline ('so their decline is not this effect'), but that separation rests on the same unconfirmed reading. A correlation of shorter output and lower accuracy is compatible with the format explanation the paper says it excludes.

title: Boxed-share changes quoted for the 'unbiased seeds' do not match the values reported for the same loop seeds
quote: against −3.7, −2.7 and −5.5 in the three unbiased seeds; pass@1
explanation: The injected-bias comparison gives -3.7, -2.7 and -5.5 as the figures in the three unbiased seeds. The gate paragraph reports boxed-share changes of -0.6, -0.6 and -5.1 for the three loop seeds on the 500 exam problems. These are the same unbiased runs (or the same design), so the two sets of numbers cannot both describe the same measure. The quantity being contrasted with the +2.8 difference is not defined: it may be a different subset of problems or a different grader. The reader cannot tell whether the bias controls were compared with the correct baseline. The comparison is the paper's only support for 'no selective avoidance', so the ambiguity matters.

title: Larger decline in the biased-verifier run is set aside as uninterpretable while smaller declines are interpreted
quote: falls 7.0 points ([−11.2, −3.0]), more than in the unbiased seeds, which we do not
explanation: In the visible-rule bias run, pass@1 falls by 7.0 points with an interval excluding zero. This is larger than in each unbiased seed (3.2-4.8). It is the one result that bears directly on the paper's question of whether a biased selection verifier hurts. The paper declines to interpret it because it is one run. The unbiased decline is built on three seeds with an interval that excludes zero and is also discussed in the abstract. Both are single-exam, single-rate results with no seed variance in the intervals. The paper does not apply the same standard to both. At minimum, the statement that the data 'neither support nor rule out' the shrinking-pool explanation (Section 5.2) should mention this run as weak but supporting evidence for harm from a biased filter.

title: Train-on-gold r_t 'drift' is not distinguishable from zero and comes from collapsed models
quote: 2.1–3.3 points (Table 5), so rt drifts as much as the falls we observe, unrelated
explanation: The text says the gold arms show r_t rises of 2.1-3.3 points, so r_t 'drifts as much as the falls we observe, unrelated to the verifier', which is used to discount the loop's r_t fall. In Table 5 every gold interval for 'all' includes zero ([-1.2, 8.1] and [-2.2, 6.7]), exactly as the loop falls (which 'reach or just touch zero') do. A drift of unknown sign is therefore compatible with no drift. The gold runs are also models whose accuracy has collapsed by about 30 points and whose style has changed. The denominator #{accepted by V'} changes sharply, so r_t movement there is not a clean baseline for the loop. The statement overreaches. The weaker honest reading is that the audit's r_t is too noisy to separate either direction.

title: 'Largest pass@1 change' of -1.3 is inconsistent with other reported changes
quote: Undecided: the pre-set pattern requires pass@1 to rise, which never happens detectably (largest pass@1
explanation: The sentence cites 'largest pass@1 change -1.3 [-8.7, +6.0]' as evidence that no pass@1 rise occurs. The final-round pass@1 changes (-4.8, -3.2, -4.2, and -7.0 in the bias run) are larger in magnitude, and the observed changes in earlier runs are not given here. 'Largest' is therefore ambiguous (largest increase? largest among the pre-final runs?). The quantity that matters for the reading rule, the largest observed increase and its interval, is not clearly reported. The interval half-width of about 7 also shows that rises of up to about +6 are compatible with this run, which is the paper's detectability point, but the sentence reads as if it supported an absence of rise.

title: Post hoc 1.7-point sample-accuracy upper limit sits beside much larger stated detectable effects
quote: of about 1.7 points is the largest upper limit among observed intervals, a
explanation: Section 5.1 reports that about 1.7 points is the largest upper limit among observed sample-accuracy intervals. The Introduction says gains of up to 4-6.5 sample-accuracy points 'could have been missed', and the design 'could detect only about 10 points of pass@1'. The paper flags that the 1.7 figure is post hoc and omits seed variance, but placing it next to the Answer to the Research Question invites a reader to take it as an upper bound on possible gains. Two incompatible detectability figures (1.7 vs 4-6.5) for the same measure are presented without a clear statement of which one a reader should use. If the intervals already exclude gains above 1.7 points on that measure, the 4-6.5 figure is overly pessimistic, and if not, the 1.7 figure is misleading.

title: Abstract says the mathematics question is unanswered, but Section 5.1 answers it ('Not detectably') and declines are measured by two graders
quote: string-match check, so neither the mathematics
explanation: The abstract and conclusion state that 'neither branch of the question is answered' because of grader dependence. Section 5.1 headlines the mathematics branch with 'Does the model get better at mathematics? Not detectably.' The second grader reproduces the sign and magnitude of the final-round declines. Only the verifier-adaptation branch is clearly unanswered (the audit is uninformative and no run varies the defect). The mathematics branch has an answer: no detectable improvement, and in the final round a decline under both graders. The summary statements overgeneralise. They should say that the mathematics branch is answered only for improvement and only under \boxed-dependent grading.

title: 'About one in six' defect rate does not match Table 5
quote: defect (about one in six correct solutions rejected)
explanation: Table 5 reports r_t for the gold-storage defect of 18.0-18.3% over all predictions at round 0, and about 19-20% among boxed predictions. That is closer to one in five than one in six (16.7%). The ratio r_t is also defined over answers accepted by V', not over 'correct solutions' in general, and it falls to 15.5-16.8% in the last round of the loop runs. The abstract figure is not tied to a specific row. The denominator and round behind 'one in six' are unclear, and the number may be a rounded form of different quantities. The effect on conclusions is small, but the headline figure should match the table.

title: Intro finished-accuracy loss range contradicts Section 4.5 and Table 2
quote: generations lose 5.5–10.6 points against the untrained model on the same problem mix
explanation: Contributions says finished generations at the highest rate lose 5.5-10.6 points (A, B, no-filter; gold about 26). Section 4.5 says they lose 1.5-9.0 points, and Table 2 'Finished, matched' at 5e-4 gives -6.1, -1.5, -4.1, -3.2 (A/B) and -9.0, -3.6 (no-filter); the largest is -9.0 and nothing reaches 10.6 or 5.5 as a minimum. Gold is -26.0 and -23.7 in Table 2, so 'about 26' is also not the range. The headline contribution overstates the effect and conflicts with the results text.

title: pass@8 'within 4 points' contradicted by Table 2 (B, seed 0 is -5.3)
quote: pass@8 ends within 4 points of round 0 in every run
explanation: Section 4.2 claims every 10^-5 run ends within 4 points of round 0 on pass@k. Table 2 shows pass@k changes of -3.3, -1.3, -5.3 (B, seed 0), -2.0 and -2.7 (C); B at seed 0 exceeds 4 points. The abstract/intro detectable-effect framing relies on small pass@k changes.

title: Two different sample-accuracy bounds (2.2 vs 1.7)
quote: about 1.7 points is the largest upper limit among observed intervals
explanation: Section 3.4 refers to 'the 2.2-point bound' on sample accuracy as a post hoc claim, while Section 5.1 calls about 1.7 points the largest upper limit among observed sample-accuracy intervals. In Table 2 the largest sample-accuracy upper limit is +1.7 (A, seed 3 at 10^-4), and no 2.2 appears. The two figures are not reconciled.

title: 'Finished accuracy carries the whole change' vs Table 2 matched values
quote: carries the whole change
explanation: Section 4.5 says at 10^-4 and 2x10^-4 finished accuracy carries the whole decline. Table 2 shows sample-accuracy falls of 2.3-4.7 (10^-4) and 6.0, 6.0 (2x10^-4) but finished-matched changes of only -1.3, -0.6, -1.0 and -2.6, -3.2, i.e. a third to a half of the fall. The statement relies on an unconditional decomposition (Table S9) that is not shown in the main text, and it reads as contradicting the matched column.

title: Replicate gap of 3.8 not derivable and not matched by same-seed pairs
quote: ends 3.8 points of sample accuracy apart
explanation: The 3.8-point replicate gap is used as the gauge of training-seed variance but the pair is not identified. Same-seed A/B pairs at 5x10^-4 differ by 2.1 (seed 1: -10.8 vs -8.7) and 4.7 (seed 2: -6.0 vs -10.7) in Table 2; A at seeds 0/1 at 10^-5 differ by 0.2. No pair in Table 2 yields 3.8, and the gap is cited again as evidence for optimistic detection thresholds.

title: 'Largest pass@1 change' wording inconsistent with data
quote:
largest pass@1
change −1.3 [−8.7, +6.0]
explanation: Section 5.1 calls -1.3 the 'largest pass@1 change' when it is the smallest in magnitude (the least negative) across Table 2, where changes reach -12.7 (C) and -12.0. Also, a nominally positive pass@k change (+2.0, 10^-4 seed 3) exists, so 'never happens detectably' applies only to interval exclusion, not to sign; the wording should say best (closest to gain) change.

title: Intro and Section 4.5 give contradictory ranges for the finished-accuracy loss at 5e-4
quote: generations lose 5.5–10.6 points against the untrained model on the same problem mix (A, B and no-ﬁlter runs; train-on-gold about 26)
explanation: Section 4.5 says the same quantity is '1.5–9.0 points, with intervals excluding zero in two of six runs'. Table 2 'Finished, matched' for A/B/no-filter at 5e-4 reads -6.1, -1.5, -4.1, -3.2, -9.0, -3.6, so the maximum is 9.0, not 10.6, and the minimum is 1.5, not 5.5. The Contribution bullet states a larger and tighter loss than the table supports, and omits that four of six intervals include zero. This is the headline decomposition contribution, and the paper does not hold it to its own descriptive-only caveat.

title: Inconsistent and unsupported 'sample-accuracy bound' (2.2 vs 1.7 points; 'largest upper limit')
quote: of about 1.7 points is the largest upper limit among observed intervals, a post hoc ﬁgure that omits seed variance, not a power statement
explanation: Section 3.4 refers to 'the 2.2-point bound', Section 5.1 to about 1.7. Table 2's sample-accuracy upper limits include +3.2, +5.2, +6.5, +4.4 (and +0.5, +1.7 at 1e-4), so no reading of 'largest upper limit' gives 1.7 or 2.2. If it means the smallest upper limit, it is a minimum over ~20 intervals chosen after the fact, i.e. the most favourable value, which is the opposite of a bound on what the data could hide. The figure is mentioned in several places as evidence for the null, so its definition and selection need to be explicit; as written it is inconsistent and cherry-picked.

title: Title and abstract call it a null while the paper's own data show significant harm; null claims lack equivalence testing and power
quote: The mean pass@1 change over the three seeds is −4.1 (t interval [−6.1, −2.1]), and −4.5 for sample accuracy ([−8.0, −1.0])
explanation: The headline is 'null result', but the final-round interval excludes zero on the negative side, and so do sample-accuracy intervals in all four A/B runs at 5e-4. The 'null' is only one-sided (no gain). 'No gain detected' is supported only by the stated MDE of ~10 points (6 final round), which is larger than gains typically reported for self-training or RLVR at this scale, and which the paper itself calls 'optimistic thresholds, not bounds'. No equivalence/non-inferiority test (e.g. TOST with a stated margin) is given, so the data neither show absence of a gain nor of a loss. The same paper that demands this standard of others reports an underpowered non-detection as a null in the title, then concedes 'we do not claim that it costs accuracy'. The framing should be 'inconclusive, point estimates negative', not 'null'.

title: Detectable-effect thresholds are computed from intervals the paper says are too narrow, yet stated in the abstract as the design's sensitivity
quote: these are optimistic thresholds, not bounds: even with h as the whole error, a gain at that size is missed 20% of the time, and probably more often
explanation: The abstract says 'The design detects only gains of about 10 points of pass@1 (6 in the ﬁnal round)' with no hedge. The paper's own evidence puts training-seed variance at the same order as h: B minus A flips from +5.3 to -5.3 on pools that differ by 0-3 examples, which implies a single-run noise SD of roughly 3.7 points (difference SD of about sqrt2 times that), against bootstrap half-widths of about 7 for pass@1. True power at a 10-point effect is therefore well below 80%. The 2.8h/1.96 formula also reuses h estimated from observed change intervals as if it were a standard error for a gain, and the '4–6.5 of sample accuracy' range is not reproducible from the half-widths in Table 2 (the largest is about 4.3).

title: Seed variance acknowledged but then ignored when reading interval-excludes-zero results and dose-response
quote: The decline may grow with the rate on one seed: at seed 1 sample accuracy falls 3.7, 6.0 and 10.8 points across the three rates, at seed 2 4.7, 6.0 and 6.0.
explanation: These differences (2-5 points between rates) are the same size as the B-A sign flip (±5.3) the paper attributes to 'trajectory noise', and each rate in the grid is one or two runs. Each seed also changes the exam partition, so a within-seed comparison across rates mixes rate with nothing else but sees one training draw per cell. The paper states the intervals 'do not include training-seed variance' but nonetheless builds claims on them: 'the sample-accuracy intervals exclude zero in all four A/B runs', 'an interval excluding zero for three of the four runs', and a monotone rate trend. In addition, 'all four A/B runs' are effectively two independent pairs ('same-seed A and B are closer to two replicates'), so the count overstates the evidence. The paper does not apply its own gauge (replicates 3.8 points apart) to these inference-style statements.

title: No multiplicity control, yet counts of intervals excluding zero are used as evidence
quote: We make no multiplicity correction and the runs are not independent (they share exam partitions and round-0 draws), so patterns across runs are descriptive, not tests.
explanation: Table 2 alone reports ~80 intervals (4 metrics, ~20 runs) plus Table 5 and the injected-bias intervals. The paper then reports tallies such as 'with an interval excluding zero for three of the four runs', 'intervals excluding zero in two of six runs' and 'one interval excludes zero and one reaches it', and reads sign consistency as a decline ('the estimates are negative in all three seeds'). Declaring a pattern 'descriptive' does not license using the tallies to support the conclusions (e.g. 'a possible small decline'); and in the opposite direction, with this many intervals, a few excluding zero are expected by chance. The correlation among runs (shared partitions, round-0 draws) is acknowledged but not modelled, e.g. by a mixed model or by pooling per-problem outcomes across runs.

title: Switch to sample accuracy as primary measure was made after seeing results and favours detecting declines
quote: pass@1 was ﬁxed in advance; sample accuracy was not, but it estimates the same quantity from all k samples with less variance, so after the runs we chose it as the primary accuracy measure
explanation: The lower-variance measure was adopted after the pre-set measures (pass@1, pass@k) gave non-significant results. Sample accuracy is the measure whose intervals most often exclude zero, so the choice raises the number of 'significant' declines (4.2: 'three of the four runs'; 4.4: 'all four'; 4.6: 'all three intervals exclude zero'). It is the same garden-of-forking-paths pattern the paper's pre-registration language is meant to avoid. Disclosure is given, but the conclusions of Section 5.1 ('Not detectably') and the final-round summary lean on this post hoc measure; a consistent standard would report the pre-set measures as the confirmatory ones and treat sample accuracy as exploratory.

title: The 'independent' second grader is not independent and cannot support the format-artefact claims
quote: It reads only the last \boxed, so a falling boxed share lowers both graders; it does not rule out a format artefact in the gate.
explanation: Both graders (V' with the gold wrapped in \boxed when the prediction contains one, and normalised string match of the last \boxed) are conditioned on the prediction containing \boxed and compare the same final string against the same stored golds. The file is even named indep_grade.py and section 5.1 reports agreement ('same sign and size') as robustness. Agreement of two boxed-dependent graders tests only the math-verify parsing step, not the shared dependence on format, normalisation and gold storage, which is the concern of the paper's title. Moreover, string match is stricter on equivalent forms (fractions, units, ordering), so a model that switches to the terse reference style (as the gate does: '$-delimited spans' 60 -> 1,577 of 1,600) can lose credit for form differences. No human or LLM-judge grading of a sample, and no gold-answer-independent check, is offered.

title: Gate failure interpreted as 'imitates terse references and loses reasoning' using the same format-sensitive graders; also based on one seed
quote: It is not a format defect: on the 500 exam problems the share of generations with a \boxed answer is unchanged (90.6 → 90.3%), accuracy among them falls from 48.5 to 17.1%, and the median length drops 3.2×
explanation: An unchanged boxed share rules out only 'no \boxed', not other format defects: the model now writes a different style (98% $-spans, 414 vs 1,332 characters), and accuracy among boxed answers is scored by the string-match grader that the paper elsewhere says is format-dependent. Shorter outputs and a lower score are also compatible with answers in a normalised-gold form (the revised recipe 'normalised gold answers') that differs from the grader's expected form, or with truncation of a final answer. The mechanism 'loses reasoning steps' is an inference from length, with no inspection of samples or a per-problem check of whether the final value is right but in a different form. The gate is a single seed with a second rate rerun, so its variance is unknown. Since the paper makes the gate decisive ('the recipe [counts] as able to help' only if it passes), the interpretation of its failure deserves the same care applied to the loop.

title: Final round: three seeds share one exam and recipe was chosen after four failed arms; the headline decline is presented without that caveat in the abstract
quote: in the ﬁnal round, with a revised recipe, pass@1 falls 3.2–4.8 points in each of three seeds (mean −4.1)
explanation: The t interval over n=3 uses 2 degrees of freedom and omits exam-draw variance ('one exam draw'). The recipe (completion-only loss, all linear layers, 1,024 cap, normalised gold, new pool) was designed after seeing every earlier arm fail and made several simultaneous changes, so it is a post hoc, multi-change configuration, tested on a gate that failed. Section 4.6 admits 'the loop's decline cannot be attributed to self-training or to the verifier', but the abstract opens with the number as if it were a clean replication. Round-0 pass@1 itself varies 46.8-49.2 across seeds from sampling alone (k=2), a 2.4-point spread comparable to the effects, which makes 'negative in all three seeds' a weaker consistency statement than it sounds.

title: Text claims pass@8 stays within 4 points in every Design I run, but Table 2 shows -5.3
quote: pass@8 ends within 4 points of round 0 in every run
explanation: Table 2 gives the 10^-5 pass@k change for B at seed 0 as -5.3 [-12.0, +2.0]. The sentence understates the largest pass@k decline in the isolated runs, in the direction that supports 'small declines'.

title: Injected-bias controls have no demonstrated sensitivity, yet their null is read as 'no selective avoidance'
quote: In neither run does the \boxed share fall selectively where boxing is penalised, so neither validates the audit.
explanation: Each control is one seed; the visible-rule control shows +2.8 [-2.8, +8.3] in share difference, so effects below roughly 5-8 points are not detectable, and the rule removes only 35 of 298 kept examples (263 kept), a small dose change. These are compared against point estimates from three unbiased seeds (-3.7, -2.7, -5.5) with no seed-variance estimate. The paper correctly says they 'neither validate the audit', but its text also says the runs 'show no selective avoidance', which a null from a control without a positive-control check cannot show. Without a positive control that the audit can detect avoidance, Table 5's near-zero changes in r_t cannot be interpreted either way; the paper's remedy ('adaptation is not excluded') is fair, but the audit is still proposed as a protocol (Section 5.3) without a demonstration that it works.

title: Audit comparison to train-on-gold r_t drift relies on point estimates whose intervals all include zero
quote: Train-on-gold, with no veriﬁer in the loop, gives rt rises of 2.1–3.3 points (Table 5), so rt drifts as much as the falls we observe, unrelated to the veriﬁer.
explanation: Both gold rows have intervals [-1.2, 8.1] and [-2.2, 6.7], which include zero, as do the self-training falls (touching zero at best). Calling this drift 'as much as' the falls treats point estimates from one seed each as equal evidence, with 2,000 resamples (fewer than the 10,000 elsewhere) and no seed variance. The three audited self-training runs are also not independent (two share the 5e-4 rate, with same-seed A/B pairs treated as near-replicates elsewhere).

title: Cap-share attribution varies from -2% to 72% across runs, undermining the 'decomposition' as a finding
quote: attributes 12–30% of the decline to the cap share in the three original seed-1 runs (and −2 and 5% in two further runs) and 52–72% at seed 2
explanation: The share of the decline attributed to cap hits ranges from negative to 72% depending on seed, with no intervals, and the conditioning ('The matched measure conditions on which problems ﬁnish after training') makes the finished-accuracy part selection-dependent. Offering this as a recommended check (ii) for others presents an unstable, post hoc, interval-free quantity as protocol; the seed-to-seed spread is itself the main finding and is evidence of the training-seed variance the intervals omit.

title: Grader dependence on the selecting verifier: exam scores use the same verifier family that selects training data, so 'Mathematics vs verifier' cannot be separated by construction
location: Section 3.4 ('Correct always means accepted by the veriﬁer'); Section 5.1
quote: “Correct” always means accepted by the veriﬁer (preset reward), the same veriﬁer that selects the training data.
explanation: The paper's central question requires an exam grader independent of the training verifier. All exam scores use V' (a patched math-verify), while the loop selected with V (or V' in the final round); the paper itself says a verifier-style adaptation would be visible only as a rise in this score. A rise could not be distinguished from verifier-specific learning, and a fall cannot be assigned to either branch; the paper concludes 'neither branch of the question is answered', which is honest but means the title question is unanswerable by design, and this was foreseeable before running (Section 3.4 states the same-verifier grading as a design choice). A held-out grader (LLM judge or human-checked sample) was not tried even on a subset.
